name: The Analytic-Synthetic Distinction
statement: Some truths hold by meaning alone; others depend on how the world is.
meaning: The analytic-synthetic distinction is a distinction between two kinds of statements or judgments. An analytic statement is one that is true, or false, by virtue of the meanings of its words alone, and can be known to be so simply by understanding those meanings, as in the stock example all bachelors are unmarried, which is true just because bachelor means unmarried man. A synthetic statement is one whose truth depends not only on the meanings of its words but on how the world actually is, so that its predicate adds content not already contained in its subject, as in all bachelors are unhappy, which is a factual claim requiring evidence. The distinction was given its influential formulation by Immanuel Kant in the Critique of Pure Reason, first published in 1781 with a second edition in 1787, where an analytic judgment is one in which the predicate is covertly contained in the concept of the subject, and a synthetic judgment is one in which it is not. Kant also famously argued for a category of the synthetic a priori, informative judgments knowable independently of experience, classing mathematics, such as seven plus five equals twelve, among them. The distinction was central to the logical positivists and was the target of W. V. O. Quine's celebrated attack, making it one of the most debated distinctions in twentieth-century philosophy.
mechanism: The analytic-synthetic distinction sorts statements by what makes them true. For an analytic statement, the meanings of the words alone settle the truth value: once you understand the terms, you can see that all bachelors are unmarried must be true, because the concept of the predicate is already contained in the concept of the subject, and its denial is a kind of contradiction. No investigation of the world is needed. For a synthetic statement, meaning is not enough: to know whether all bachelors are unhappy, or that a particular object is heavy, one must consult how things actually stand, because the predicate adds information not contained in the subject. Kant articulated this as containment, the predicate B belonging to the subject A as something covertly thought within the concept A in analytic judgments, and lying outside it in synthetic ones. The distinction interlocks with two others often run alongside it: the a priori versus a posteriori distinction, concerning how a statement is known, independently of experience or on the basis of it, and the necessary versus contingent distinction, concerning its modal status, true in all possible worlds or not. Traditionally, the analytic was aligned with the a priori and the necessary. Kant disrupted the neat alignment by asserting synthetic a priori judgments, informative yet knowable without experience. Quine later attacked the distinction itself, arguing that analyticity cannot be defined without circularity and that no statement is immune from revision, a doctrine he called confirmation holism.

examples.text: All bachelors are unmarried is true by meaning alone; understanding the words suffices to know it.
All bachelors are unhappy depends on how the world is, and requires evidence to assess.
Kant classed seven plus five equals twelve as synthetic a priori, informative yet knowable independently of experience.

variants.name: The three distinctions
variants.text: Analytic versus synthetic, a priori versus a posteriori, and necessary versus contingent, traditionally aligned but distinct.

variants.name: The synthetic a priori
variants.text: Kant's controversial category of informative judgments, such as those of mathematics, knowable independently of experience.

whyItMatters: The analytic-synthetic distinction is one of the most important and contested distinctions in the philosophy of language and the theory of knowledge. It offers a way to separate truths that hold by meaning alone from truths that depend on the world, and thereby bears directly on the nature of a priori knowledge, on the status of logic and mathematics, and on what philosophy itself can hope to establish by analysis. Kant's formulation, and especially his claim that there are synthetic a priori judgments, framed the agenda of modern epistemology and motivated his whole critical project. The logical positivists of the Vienna Circle built their philosophy on the distinction, treating logic and mathematics as analytic and holding that all other meaningful statements must be empirically verifiable, and they used it to try to expel metaphysics as meaningless. Quine's Two Dogmas of Empiricism, which argued that the distinction is an unfounded dogma, was one of the most influential papers of twentieth-century philosophy and reshaped debates about meaning, analyticity, and holism.

working.text: ask whether the truth of a statement is settled by the meanings of its words alone.
call it analytic if meaning suffices, synthetic if its truth also depends on how the world is.
note the traditional alignment of analytic with a priori and necessary, and Kant's disrupting synthetic a priori.

limits: The analytic-synthetic distinction, long treated as fundamental, was famously challenged by W. V. O. Quine in his 1951 paper Two Dogmas of Empiricism, which called it one of the unfounded dogmas of empiricism. Quine argued that there is no non-circular way to define analyticity, because the cluster of notions used to explain it, synonymy, definition, meaning, only define one another in a closed circle, and that no statement is in principle immune from revision in light of experience. His alternative was confirmation holism, the view that our statements face the tribunal of experience not one by one but only as a corporate body, so that the sharp line between the analytic and the synthetic cannot be drawn. Defenders have replied that the distinction can be salvaged or that Quine's demands are too strict, and the debate remains unsettled. The three distinctions must also be kept apart, since Kant and later Kripke showed that analytic, a priori, and necessary do not simply coincide.
misreadings: The analytic-synthetic distinction is not the same as the a priori and a posteriori distinction, which concerns how a statement is known rather than what makes it true, nor the same as necessary versus contingent, which concerns modal status; the three were traditionally aligned but are logically distinct. Kant's synthetic a priori shows the analytic is not the only source of a priori knowledge. And the distinction is not beyond challenge, since Quine argued analyticity cannot be non-circularly defined, so treating it as identical to the a priori, as exhausting a priori knowledge, or as unassailable, misreads a fundamental but contested distinction.
origin: A distinction between statements true by meaning alone and statements whose truth depends on the world, given its influential form by Kant in the Critique of Pure Reason and later attacked by W. V. O. Quine.

sources.text: The Analytic/Synthetic Distinction, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — analytic sentences as true by virtue of the meanings of their words alone, Kant's containment formulation and the synthetic a priori, the relation to the a priori and the necessary, and Quine's attack on the distinction in Two Dogmas of Empiricism.

A Priori Justification and Knowledge, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the relation of the analytic/synthetic distinction to the a priori/a posteriori and necessary/contingent distinctions, and the prying apart of these distinctions by Kripke and Putnam.
